text: One man stood at the center of this storm and would not move.
Jesse Binga came to Chicago in 1892, worked his way up from peddling and Pullman cars, and built a real estate fortune.
In 1908 he opened the city's first Black-owned bank.
In 1917 he bought a house at 5922 South Park Avenue, on a white block.
His home and his offices were bombed at least five times between 1917 and 1921.
He refused to leave.
I will not run, he said, and he stayed.
His story did not end in triumph.
When the Depression hit, his bank, heavily invested in mortgages to Black churches and families, was shut down by the state in 1930.
Binga lost everything, was convicted of embezzlement, and went to Joliet prison in 1935 at the age of 70.
The same neighbors who had banked with him signed a petition for his release, and he was paroled in 1938 and pardoned in 1941.
He died in 1950, largely forgotten, in the city he had helped build.
His house still stands.
Hold that picture in mind, a man who would not run from a bomb, because it shows what the next weapon was designed to avoid.
There would be no more single defiant homeowners to rally around.
The fight would move from the doorstep to the deed.
After the riot, white Chicago reached for a quieter and more durable weapon than the bomb.
The racially restrictive covenant.
A covenant was a clause written into a property deed.
It barred the owner from selling, leasing, or even allowing occupancy to anyone who was not white, with narrow exceptions for live-in servants.
